headline: CRISP matched a senior specialist during fast surgery checks.

heroVisual.alt: Illustration of a magnifying glass examining the evidence behind an AI headline in a newspaper.

the_story:
During surgery, a pathologist — a specialist who examines tissue to help identify disease — may need an answer before the next step. A frozen section is tissue quickly frozen, sliced and examined during surgery. Usual preparation preserves it in chemicals and wax first, giving it a different appearance.

CRISP analyses those images. In an observational study, meaning researchers watched normal care, it beat other AI models. A separate reader study found it matched the senior specialist overall.
laidies_read: This was a comparison in a difficult setting: the image must be read quickly while surgery is underway. CRISP gives a prediction; the pathologist still interprets the tissue and informs the surgical team. The paper describes it as decision support, not a replacement for the specialist.
what_this_means: This does not show that CRISP improves treatment or patient outcomes. The study observed performance and included a simulated deployment analysis. The authors say they still need a study that changes care and follows what happens to patients.
cocktail_party: “CRISP matched a senior tissue specialist and beat the other AI models compared. That is still different from proving better care.”
class_notes: AI Fundamentals 101: Why Benchmarks Are Useful But Flawed explains that a result describes the task and conditions tested. It does not establish readiness for a different real-world job. That distinction matters when reading this study.

sources.label: Nature Medicine — A clinically-oriented foundation model for intraoperative pathology
